item.title: Asuka-nabe: The Ancient Milk Hot Pot of Asuka — Guide
item.description: Asuka-nabe is one of Japan’s most unusual regional hot pots: a chicken-and-vegetable nabe simmered in a broth enriched with milk, giving it a mellow, creamy character unlike any other Japanese pot. Its origins are traced to the Asuka period over 1,300 years ago, when dairy foods and cattle-keeping were introduced to Japan from the Asian mainland via the imperial court based in Asuka — making this humble dish a living echo of Japan’s very first encounter with milk.

item.title: Asuka: Cradle of the Japanese State and Its Ancient Tombs — Guide
item.description: Asuka, a quiet farming village south of Kashihara, was the political heart of Japan in the 6th and 7th centuries, before the capital moved to Nara — the era when Buddhism and continental culture first took root and the imperial state was forged. Its gentle countryside is scattered with the enigmatic remains of that dawn age: ancient temple sites, mysterious carved granite stones whose purpose is still debated, decorated tomb mounds, and above all the Ishibutai Kofun, a monumental 7th-century burial chamber whose earth mound has eroded away to reveal enormous megaliths, the largest weighing some 77 tons.

item.title: Nara Haunted Spots: Ancient Burial Mounds, Forgotten Temples & Ghost Legends
item.description: Nara is Japan’s oldest civilised landscape — a basin ringed by mountains where emperors ruled, monks withdrew, and entire capitals were built and abandoned within decades. That history leaves a particular weight on the land. The burial mounds of unknown occupants, the sealed tomb chambers, the primeval forests that humans have never felled, the ruins of palaces visible only as foundation stones in empty fields — these are not jump-scare haunted houses.

item.title: Nara Hidden Gems: Asuka, Muro-ji, Tanzan Shrine & Ancient Sites Beyond the Park
item.description: The Nara that most visitors see — the deer, Todai-ji, Kasuga Taisha — represents perhaps 10% of the prefecture’s heritage. Spread across the Yamato Plain and into the surrounding mountains is a landscape of extraordinary archaeological and cultural density: Japan’s first capitals, the oldest Buddhist temples, burial mounds that predate written Japanese history, mountain shrines of mythological antiquity, and a merchant town so intact it makes Kyoto’s Gion feel modern. These are the sites that reward the traveller willing to go one train stop further.
